Chapter 10—Creating New Rituals: Personalizing the Goodbye.
Sometimes, the old ways just don’t fit. Maybe the traditions we’ve grown up with feel a little distant—like they belong to someone else’s story, not ours. When that happens, there’s actually an opening. A chance to create something new... something that really feels like it belongs to you.
Picture this: a father, heartbroken after losing his son, finds no comfort in the traditional funeral. The words seem empty. The rituals just don’t connect. So, he gathers his family and friends at a park, right under the trees his son loved most. They share stories, play his favorite songs, and plant a tree in his memory. It’s simple—but it fits. In that moment, the goodbye feels real. It’s not just about tradition; it’s about honoring the person they love.
All over the world, people are inventing new ways to mourn. Some write letters to the ones they’ve lost, leaving them with the body or burning them as a final goodbye. Others create art, music, or even gardens as living tributes. Each ritual is different, just as unique as the person being remembered. But they all have something in common: the need to remember, to honor, and to find meaning in loss.
For many, building a new ritual is actually empowering. It lets you take control—turning the process of mourning into something personal. And honestly, these rituals don’t need to be expensive or complicated. What matters most is that they feel true to you.
Imagine a group of friends, spread out across the country. When one of them passes away, they hold a virtual memorial. Everyone shares photos, tells their favorite stories, and lights a candle at home. The experience is bittersweet, but it brings comfort. Even though they’re miles apart, their connection is real.
Now, starting a new ritual isn’t always easy. There can be pushback—from family, from tradition, or even from that little voice inside that worries about doing it wrong. But here’s the thing: taking that leap, inventing your own way to say goodbye, can be a kind of healing all on its own. It helps you make sense of loss, and it’s a powerful way to honor the bonds that last, even after someone is gone.
